planting.note: Plant small pot-grown divisions in spring into a gritty, humus-rich scree or trough mix that stays lightly moist; unlike many scree alpines it resents baking dry.

directions: Spring gentian forms a tiny tuft of glossy leaf rosettes that disappears each April beneath disproportionately large, five-pointed, intensely saturated blue starflowers held almost at ground level. It is widespread across the Alps, Pyrenees, and Apennines but also turns up famously far from the mountains on limestone turf in the Burren of Ireland and Upper Teesdale in England, a distribution botanists still find striking. Grow it in a lean but never bone-dry scree or trough, keeping some moisture at the root through spring growth, and treat individual rosettes as relatively short-lived, replacing a planting from self-sown seedlings or fresh divisions every few years. Full sun suits it in cooler climates, but give light shade where summer heat is intense.

planting.note: Plant divisions or pot-grown starts in spring into gritty, distinctly alkaline soil in full sun; this species specifically wants limestone, unlike its acid-loving relative Gentiana acaulis.

directions: Clusius' gentian produces the same large, upward-facing deep-blue trumpets as the better-known stemless gentian, but is the calcicole counterpart of that acid-loving species, occurring naturally on limestone pastures and rocky turf throughout the Alps and Pyrenees. It is named for the 16th-century botanist Carolus Clusius, one of the first Europeans to systematically describe alpine flora. Site it in a scree bed or trough built with limestone chips rather than the lime-free grit used for acaulis, in full sun with sharp drainage, and avoid disturbing established clumps since they resent root interference. Flowering is heaviest in late spring, slightly later than most of its stemless-gentian relatives.

planting.note: Root non-flowering rosette cuttings and set into a vertical limestone crevice or tufa block in spring; this cushion species is propagated almost exclusively by cuttings rather than seed in cultivation.

directions: Vandelli's rock jasmine builds a hard, flattened silver-gray cushion of minute, densely hairy rosettes packed tightly against limestone cliff crevices in the Alps and Pyrenees, named for the 18th-century botanist Domenico Vandelli. In early summer the cushion is dotted with small, nearly stemless white flowers with a contrasting yellow eye, produced singly from each rosette rather than in showy clusters. It demands a vertical or steeply tilted crevice, tufa block, or deep scree with maximum air movement and alkaline grit, since the dense hairy surface traps moisture that quickly causes rot if the crown stays wet over winter. Increase named forms from rooted cuttings taken from non-flowering shoots rather than disturbing the parent cushion.

planting.note: Plant rooted rosette cuttings in spring into a deep, lime-free scree or moraine bed; this is one of the most difficult true high-alpines to maintain outside a specialist alpine-house scree frame.

directions: Alpine rock jasmine grows naturally on acidic, constantly moving screes and moraines near the Alps' highest summits, often above 3,000 meters, where it is buried under a long, insulating snowpack for most of the year. It forms a tiny, loose cushion of narrow rosettes that in midsummer bear small pink flowers fading to white with age. Because lowland gardens cannot replicate its deep, stable snow cover, it is notoriously short-lived outside a dedicated scree frame or alpine house with scrupulous summer drainage and winter protection from alternating freeze-thaw; most growers treat it as a specialist challenge rather than a reliable garden plant. Propagate only from rooted non-flowering shoots, since the taproot resents any disturbance.

planting.note: Plant dormant corms or pot-grown starts in fall into a gritty scree or trough that floods briefly with snowmelt in spring but dries completely by summer; mimics the vernal-pool flats of its native high desert.

directions: Short-sepal bitterroot is a deciduous relative of the showier evergreen lewisias, native to shallow, seasonally flooded flats and open pine-juniper woodland from Arizona and California north into Oregon and Nevada. It flowers unusually early for the genus, pushing up large, satiny white to pale lavender-pink blooms directly from a resting corm as soon as snowmelt saturates the ground, then dies back completely and disappears underground through the dry summer months. Give it generous moisture only during its brief spring growth cycle in a gritty, fast-draining scree or trough, and keep it bone dry the rest of the year so the corm does not rot in summer heat. Because the whole plant vanishes by early summer, mark its location so the resting corm isn't disturbed or mistaken for an empty spot.

planting.note: Plant into a tufa wall crevice or constantly seeping rock crevice in spring; unusual among lewisias, this species wants steady moisture at the root year-round, not summer drought.

directions: Cantelow's lewisia is one of the genus's oddities, growing naturally on wet, mossy cliff faces and seasonal waterfall seeps in a few northern California counties rather than the dry scree favored by most of its relatives. Its evergreen rosettes send up branching sprays of deep pink, darker-veined flowers in summer, blooming noticeably later than Lewisia cotyledon and its hybrids. Because the species evolved anchored in rock cracks with constant seepage, it performs best on a tufa wall or in a crevice with a slow, steady trickle of water, paired with sharp drainage so the moisture never stagnates around the crown. Light shade through the hottest part of the day helps recreate the cool, humid cliff-face conditions of its native habitat.

planting.note: Divide or plant rooted sections in spring into a gritty, alkaline scree, trough, or tufa crevice in full sun to light shade; this is one of the earliest-flowering true alpine Kabschia saxifrages.

directions: Burser's saxifrage is one of the classic Kabschia group cushion saxifrages, native to limestone cliffs and rock crevices of the Eastern Alps, forming a dense hummock of tiny, spine-tipped silver-gray rosettes. It is famous among alpine growers for flowering astonishingly early, often pushing large white flowers on short red stems through late winter snow cover weeks before most other rock garden plants stir. Grow it in a sharply drained, alkaline scree, trough, or tufa crevice with morning sun but shelter from the hottest afternoon sun in warm climates, since Kabschia saxifrages scorch easily in summer heat. Top-dress with limestone grit annually and divide congested cushions after flowering to renew vigor and propagate named forms.
